# What Is a Press Release, and When Is It Worth It?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-press-release/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-02 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: A press release is a short, formal announcement a company issues to the media, and increasingly to the public directly, about something it wants known. It is a canonical record of the facts, not a marketing channel and not coverage. Journalists still rely on PR material, but Cision's 2026 survey of 1,899 journalists found only 22% wanted more press releases, against 47% wanting data or research, and 82% rejected pitches for being irrelevant. Issue a release when the news is material and citable, write it plainly, and do the pitching separately.

## Key points

- A release puts the facts of an announcement in one quotable place, with a named person to call.
- For US listed companies, a release through a widely circulated wire is one recognised way to make material information public under Regulation FD.
- Coverage comes from a story a journalist wants, a relationship and a pitch; the release is the supporting document.
- Journalists ask PR for data, early access and experts more than for releases.
- Skip releases for feature updates, opinions, momentum announcements without numbers, or filling a quiet month.

The press release has existed for over a century, and it survives because it does one job well: it puts the facts of an announcement in one canonical, quotable place, with a named person to call. Everything else people expect from it is usually misplaced.

## What a press release is for

**It records the facts.** A journalist, partner, investor or customer who wants to know exactly what was announced, by whom, on what date and with what quotations, can find it in one place. That is why releases are structured the way they are.

| Part | What it contains | Common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Headline | The news, in plain words | A slogan or an adjective |
| Dateline | City and date of issue | Missing, so the release cannot be placed in time |
| Lead paragraph | Who, what, when, where and why, in one or two sentences | Background before the news |
| Supporting detail | Numbers, terms, availability, context | Unsubstantiated superlatives |
| Quotation | One named executive saying something a person would say | Three quotes of corporate boilerplate |
| Boilerplate | A short, factual paragraph about the company | A mission statement |
| Contact | A named person with an email and phone number | A general inbox |

**It signals seriousness.** Some announcements, a funding round, a regulated product launch, a senior hire, a partnership with a public company, are expected to have a release, and their absence looks odd.

**It can meet a legal disclosure standard.** For US public companies, Regulation FD, adopted by the SEC in August 2000, bars selective disclosure of material information to analysts and investors. Law firm Goodwin's guide notes that filing a Form 8-K is generally the most reliable way to make information public, but that "a press release issued through a widely circulated news or wire service" is a recognised alternative. An executive's personal social post, on its own, does not count. Private companies are not bound by Regulation FD, but investors and partners often hold them to similar expectations.

**It creates a durable, indexed record.** Releases distributed through wire services are picked up by financial data terminals, news aggregators and search engines, and increasingly by the systems that feed AI answer engines. A release is one of the few pieces of company-authored text that third parties will republish verbatim. Our piece on [how LLMs choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) covers why plain, factual, dated text tends to be cited.

## What a press release is not

**It is not coverage.** Issuing a release does not make anyone write about you. Cision's 2026 State of the Media report found most journalists sort through more than 50 pitches a week, and 72% said fewer than a quarter of the pitches they receive are relevant. Coverage comes from a story a journalist wants, a relationship and a pitch, of which the release is the supporting document.

**It is not a marketing channel.** Nobody's customer acquisition plan should contain "issue press releases." The readers of wire services are journalists, analysts and bots.

**It is not a place for adjectives.** The release that describes the company as a leading, innovative, next-generation platform is signalling to every journalist that it contains no news. In Cision's survey, 53% of journalists said they reject pitches for being too promotional or sales-focused.

## What journalists say they want

Cision's survey asks journalists what they want from PR and why they reject pitches. It is vendor research from a company that sells PR software and wire distribution, so read it as a well-sampled view of journalist preferences rather than neutral measurement.

| What journalists want PR to send more of | Share |
| --- | --- |
| Data or original research | 47% |
| Embargoed or early access information | 45% |
| Access to experts or interviews | 42% |
| Press releases | 22% |

| Why journalists reject a pitch | Share |
| --- | --- |
| Not relevant to their audience or coverage | 82% |
| Too promotional or sales-focused | 53% |
| No clear news angle or point of view | 34% |
| Too generic or mass-email feel | 27% |

Two lessons follow. The release is necessary but not sufficient: it records the news, and the pitch, the data and the expert make the story. And relevance dominates everything else, which is a targeting problem rather than a writing problem. Cision's report puts the pitch sweet spot at around 100 to 200 words, sent by email, which 97% of journalists prefer.

> A release guarantees distribution, not attention.

## How distribution works

**Wire services** charge a fee to push the release to newsrooms, terminals and aggregators. Prices vary widely with geographic reach, length and multimedia, so get quotes for the specific circuit you need. They guarantee distribution, not attention.

**Direct pitching** sends a short personal note, with the release attached or linked, to specific journalists who cover the beat. This is where coverage actually comes from, and it is the part PR agencies are paid for.

**Owned publication** posts the release on the company's own newsroom page, which is the canonical version everything else should link to. Our guide to [paid, earned, shared and owned media](https://lowob.com/research/paid-earned-shared-owned-media/) explains why that owned copy matters.

## When to issue one, and when not to bother

| Issue a release | Do not bother |
| --- | --- |
| Money raised, with amount and lead investor | Feature updates |
| A product a regulated audience needs the facts on | Blog-post-sized opinions |
| A senior appointment | "Momentum" announcements with no number |
| A partnership with a party whose name carries weight | Anything you would be embarrassed to see quoted in full |
| A milestone with a verifiable number | Filling a quiet month |
| A partner, investor or exchange expects one | Announcements nobody outside the company would act on |

Each item in the right-hand column costs money, trains journalists to ignore the company and produces a search result the company will later wish were something else.

## The **lowob** rule for releases

Write them in the plainest language available, with the news in the first sentence, one quotation a human would actually say, and a number wherever one can be substantiated. Put the canonical version on your own site. Use a wire only when the announcement is material. Bring something journalists ask for, data, early access or an expert, to the pitch. And never confuse the release with the work of getting someone to care. For the positioning the release should express, see [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/).

## lowob takeaways

- **The release is the record.** Facts, date, quote and contact in one place.
- **The pitch is the work.** Coverage comes from relevance to a specific journalist's beat.
- **Bring what journalists want.** Data, early access and experts beat a longer release.
- **Use the wire for material news.** Everything else goes on your own newsroom page or nowhere.

## Common questions

### Does a press release get you media coverage?

Not by itself. Journalists receive far more pitches than they can use; in Cision's 2026 survey, 72% said fewer than a quarter of pitches were relevant. Coverage comes from a relevant pitch, a relationship and a story, with the release as the supporting document.

### When should a company issue a press release?

When the announcement is material, such as money raised, a regulated product launch, a senior appointment, a weighty partnership or a verifiable milestone, or when a partner, investor or exchange expects one.

### What should a press release contain?

A headline, dateline, a lead paragraph with who, what, when, where and why, supporting detail, one quotation from a named executive, a short boilerplate paragraph about the company, and a named contact.

### Is a press release still relevant in 2026?

Yes, as a canonical, citable record that wires, terminals, search engines and AI answer engines republish, and as a recognised disclosure route for US listed companies. It is not relevant as an acquisition channel.

## Next Move

Before your next announcement, write the first sentence of the release and ask whether a journalist on your beat would act on it. If not, put it on your newsroom page, skip the wire, and spend the budget on one piece of data worth pitching.
